title: Check yourself: what the Space does with your entries

questions.stem: A switch keeps the host link's routing mode, primary or standby, under one Space key. The failover QBean writes the new mode with push each time it switches, and participants read the mode with rdp. Over a year without a restart the link switches 3,000 times. What do the participants read, and what does the key hold?

options.text: The latest mode, since push puts it at the head, and the key holds an entry for every switch
options.says: push inserts at the head without removing anything, so readers see the newest and the old entries pile up

options.text: The latest mode, since push replaces what the key held, and the key holds a single entry
options.says: only put replaces the entries under a key; push adds one at the head

options.text: The first mode ever written, since rdp returns the oldest entry, and the key holds an entry for every switch
options.says: rdp returns the head, and push puts each new mode there

options.text: The first mode ever written, since push adds behind it, and the key holds a single entry
options.says: out adds behind the oldest entry; push adds in front of it, and nothing removes the old ones

origin.section: 12.1 A Key Holds a Queue: `out` Adds, `put` Replaces, `push` Goes First

questions.stem: A QBean's thread loops on sp.in("settlement.jobs") with no timeout, and its stopService clears the loop's running flag. The QBean is undeployed at 18:00 while the queue is empty and deployed again at 18:05. At 19:00 a job is queued. What happens to it?

options.text: The new deployment's thread takes it, since the old thread ended when its flag was cleared
options.says: a thread waiting inside an untimed in never gets back to the loop to see the flag

options.text: The new deployment's thread takes it, since Q2 interrupts the threads of a QBean it undeploys
options.says: the old thread was still waiting after the stop; nothing ended its wait

options.text: Either thread may take it, since the old thread is still waiting in in on the same key
options.says: the undeployed component's thread outlives the undeploy and competes with the new one

options.text: Both threads may take a copy of it, since in hands the entry to every thread waiting on the key
options.says: in takes the entry; one waiting thread gets it and the other keeps waiting

origin.section: 12.2 A Wait Without a Timeout and an Entry Without a Lease Both Last Forever

questions.stem: To keep an audit trail, a team registers a SpaceListener on the txnmgr queue. Its notify writes one row to an audit database, and under load each row takes about 200 ms. What happens to the answers terminals get?

options.text: Each comes about 200 ms later, since notify runs on the session thread that wrote the Context
options.says: the listener runs inside out on the writer's thread, here the QServer session, which reads nothing more meanwhile

options.text: Each comes about 200 ms later, since the TransactionManager waits for every listener before taking the Context
options.says: the TransactionManager knows nothing of listeners; the delay is in the writer's call to out

options.text: They come as fast as before, since listeners run on a thread that belongs to the space
options.says: TSpace calls listeners on the thread that wrote the entry

options.text: They come as fast as before, since a listener works on a copy after the Context has gone
options.says: the listener is called during out, before the writer can go on

origin.section: 12.4 A Listener Runs on the Writer's Thread and Takes Nothing

questions.stem: A participant keeps each terminal's purchase count for the day in a Serializable object under count.<terminal>. For each purchase it reads the object with rdp and adds one to its field. The tests use tspace:default and pass; production uses je:velocity. After a terminal's 50th purchase today, what does the stored count say?

options.text: 50, since a read returns the stored object in either kind of space
options.says: that holds only for tspace:; je: deserializes a new copy on every read

options.text: 50, since je: writes a changed object back when the participant returns
options.says: nothing writes the copy back; only an explicit out, put or push stores it

options.text: Its starting count, since each read from je: returns a copy that is then dropped
options.says: the change reached only a copy, so the stored object never moves

options.text: Its starting count, since je: refuses changes to an object once it is stored
options.says: je: refuses nothing here; the change is made to a copy, which is then thrown away

origin.section: 12.5 A Transient Space Hands Back the Stored Object, and a Persistent One a Copy
